lessons.title: Choosing Your Regime While Filing Your Income Tax Return

children.text: Everything you declared to your employer was provisional. The return is where your regime becomes final. For a salaried taxpayer it comes down to one question on the e-filing portal, a few schedules and a verification step that many people forget. This lesson walks you through filing day so that the regime you worked out on paper is the one the tax department actually applies.

body.text: Your Form 16 tells you what your employer assumed. Your return tells the tax department what is true. If the two disagree, the return wins.

children.text: Step 0: Pick the Right Return Form

body.caption: Which ITR Form Fits You (As Used Under the 1961 Act)

Salary plus capital gains beyond ITR-1 limits, more than one house property, or income above ₹50 lakh
Answer the opt-out question in the return

Quote the option form acknowledgement filed before the due date

body.title: Which Form?
body.question: Shreya, a salaried analyst in Kochi earning ₹14 lakh, sold shares this year for ₹80,000 of short-term gains. She has no business income. Which return form should she use?
options: ITR-1, because her income is below ₹50 lakh
ITR-2, because short-term capital gains are not allowed in ITR-1
ITR-3, because share trading is business income
ITR-4, because she has investment income
body.explanation: ITR-1 allows only long-term gains on listed equity up to ₹1.25 lakh. Short-term gains push her to ITR-2. Occasional delivery-based share sales are capital gains, not business income, so ITR-3 is not needed.

children.text: Collect Form 16 from every employer you worked for during the year.
Download your AIS and Form 26AS from the e-filing portal and note every interest, dividend and TDS entry.
Rerun your regime comparison with the full-year numbers, including income your employer never saw.
In the return, answer the question asking whether you wish to opt out of the new tax regime. Yes means old regime. No, the default, means new regime.
If you chose the old regime, enter HRA and LTA as exempt allowances and fill the deductions schedule for 80C, 80D and the rest. In the new regime, most of these fields are disabled.
Check the tax computation page against your own calculation. Pay any balance as self-assessment tax before submitting.
Submit by the due date and e-verify with Aadhaar OTP or net banking immediately.

body.text: The opt-out question is worded in terms of leaving the new regime because the new regime is the default. Read it carefully. Answering Yes when you meant to stay in the new regime is a common slip, and it silently switches your whole computation to old regime slabs.

body.caption: Total tax is computed under the regime you select in the return, not the one your employer used.

body.label: Arnav's refund from the TDS lesson
body.context: His employer deducted ₹2,57,400 under the old regime after rejecting his proofs. He selects the new regime in his return, where his tax is ₹97,500.

children.text: The opposite also happens. Sonal, a supply chain manager in Vadodara, earns ₹14,00,000 and her employer deducted ₹81,900 of TDS under the new regime. Her AIS shows ₹60,000 of FD interest and ₹12,000 of savings account interest that she never told payroll about.

body.title: What Does Sonal Still Owe?
body.prompt: Sonal stays in the new regime. Including the ₹72,000 of interest, what balance tax, including cess, must she pay before filing?
body.explanation: Taxable income is ₹14,00,000 minus ₹75,000 plus ₹72,000, which is ₹13,97,000. Slab tax is ₹60,000 plus 15% of ₹1,97,000 (₹29,550), total ₹89,550. Cess is ₹3,582, so total tax is ₹93,132. After ₹81,900 of TDS, she owes ₹11,232 as self-assessment tax, plus any interest for not paying it through the year.

body.title: What if your AIS shows income that is wrong?

children.text: AIS is built from what banks, brokers and employers report against your PAN. It can contain duplicates, an FD reported twice, or income belonging to a joint holder. Do not simply ignore it. Use the feedback option in AIS to mark the entry as duplicate, incorrect or belonging to someone else, and keep supporting statements. Then report the correct figure in your return.
The reverse is more dangerous. If your AIS shows interest or dividends and your return does not, the mismatch is flagged automatically and usually leads to a notice.

Includes only proofs your employer accepted
A starting point, not a final answer

columns.label: Your income tax return

Can include genuine deductions your employer missed, with documents

body.title: Form 16 Says Old, Farah Wants New
body.scenario: Farah, a Chennai-based pharmacist at a hospital chain, declared the old regime in April. Her Form 16 shows ₹1,50,000 of 80C and ₹1,20,000 of HRA exemption. When she reruns the numbers at filing time, the new regime is cheaper. On the portal, the pre-filled data shows the old regime exemptions, and the deductions fields go grey when she answers No to the opt-out question. She worries that the mismatch with Form 16 will trigger a notice.
body.prompt: Is Farah doing anything wrong, and what should she check?
body.modelAnswer: No. As a salaried employee with no business income, she is entitled to pick the new regime in her return even though her employer used the old one. The greyed-out fields are the portal correctly removing deductions that are not allowed in the new regime. She should make sure the HRA exemption is not carried into her salary schedule, so her full HRA is shown as taxable salary. She should confirm her gross salary matches Form 16 and her AIS, and check the tax computation page. Because her TDS was calculated under the old regime, which she has found to be the costlier one, her TDS will usually exceed her new regime tax and she will get a refund. If her AIS shows extra income that pushes her tax above TDS, she pays the balance before filing. The regime difference itself is not a mismatch.

children.text: The Verification Step That Can Cost You the Old Regime

stats.label: Return due date
stats.context: For most salaried taxpayers without audit

stats.label: Belated return deadline
stats.context: New regime only, for non-business taxpayers

body.text: Uploading a return is not the same as filing it. Under the rules applied under the 1961 Act, if you e-verify after 30 days, the date of verification is treated as the date of filing. A return uploaded on 25 July but verified on 10 September becomes a late return. For a taxpayer without business income, that can mean losing the old regime for the year, plus a late fee. Verify the same day you upload.

body.title: Don't Forget to Verify
body.textWithBlank: After uploading your return, you must e-verify it within ___ days, or the verification date is treated as your filing date.
body.explanation: Aadhaar OTP, net banking, a pre-validated bank account or a demat account can be used to e-verify instantly. Do it as soon as you upload.

cards.definition: Employer's annual TDS certificate showing salary, exemptions allowed and TDS. Based on your declared regime.
Annual Information Statement. Everything reported against your PAN: salary, interest, dividends, share sales, TDS.
Statement of tax credits against your PAN, including TDS, TCS, advance tax and self-assessment tax.
The return question asking if you wish to opt out of the new regime. Yes selects the old regime.
Balance tax you pay yourself before filing, when TDS and advance tax fall short.
Confirming your return by Aadhaar OTP or net banking, within 30 days of upload.

body.label: Income Tax e-Filing Portal
body.description: Download AIS and Form 26AS, file your return, choose your regime and e-verify in one place.

body.title: Your Filing Day Checklist
steps: Download Form 16 from every employer and your AIS and Form 26AS
Reconcile all interest, dividends and capital gains in AIS with your own records
Rerun the regime comparison with full-year figures
Choose the correct ITR form for your income
Answer the opt-out question deliberately, then check the deductions schedule matches your regime
Pay any balance as self-assessment tax and enter the challan details
Submit before 31 July and e-verify the same day

points: Your regime becomes final in your return, not in your employer's declaration or Form 16.
Salaried taxpayers without business income choose the regime by answering the opt-out question in ITR-1 or ITR-2.
Picking a different regime from your employer is allowed and often leads to a refund or a small balance payable.
Always reconcile with AIS, since interest and dividends your employer never saw still have to be taxed.
Upload by the due date and e-verify within 30 days, or your return can be treated as late and the old regime lost.
Pay any shortfall as self-assessment tax before submitting.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not tax advice. Return forms, questions, deadlines and verification rules are described as they operated under the Income-tax Act, 1961 and may change for returns filed under the Income-tax Act, 2025. Check the e-filing portal for your tax year and consult a qualified tax professional.
